## The idea

A *canon* asks one melody to accompany itself. A second voice enters with the
same subject after a delay, and later voices may follow in turn. The program can
express this in a few lines, but the melody carries an unusual burden: its later
notes must form convincing vertical intervals against its earlier ones.

Entry delay decides which positions in the subject overlap. Transposition then
changes the interval produced at every one of those meetings. An arbitrary
pair of values may expose repeated seconds, crowd the voices into one register,
or cause every cadence to arrive against ongoing motion. Such a result is
useful evidence. It shows that a canonic subject contains the seeds of its own
accompaniment rather than becoming contrapuntal through delay alone.

Begin with untransposed entries one full bar apart. Once that baseline is
audible, vary delay and transposition separately so their effects do not become
confused. Each voice runs in its own thread. The subject array remains shared
score data, while entry time, register, synth, and amplitude belong to the
description of each follower.

## Run this

The subject occupies four beats. Three voices enter at four-beat intervals,
with the third placed an octave lower. Every voice repeats the same data sixteen
times, so after the final entry the complete three-part texture continues long
enough for its overlapping pattern to become familiar.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 96

subject = [
  {note: 60, start: 0.0, duration: 0.5},
  {note: 64, start: 0.5, duration: 0.5},
  {note: 67, start: 1.0, duration: 1.0},
  {note: 65, start: 2.0, duration: 0.5},
  {note: 64, start: 2.5, duration: 0.5},
  {note: 62, start: 3.0, duration: 0.5},
  {note: 60, start: 3.5, duration: 0.5}
]

define :play_events do |events, transpose_by, amp|
  cursor = 0.0
  events.each do |event|
    sleep event[:start] - cursor
    play event[:note] + transpose_by,
      release: event[:duration] * 0.8,
      amp: amp
    cursor = event[:start]
  end
  sleep events.last[:duration]
end

entries = [
  {delay: 0, transpose: 0, synth: :piano, amp: 0.85},
  {delay: 4, transpose: 0, synth: :pluck, amp: 0.65},
  {delay: 8, transpose: -12, synth: :hollow, amp: 0.5}
]

entries.each do |entry|
  in_thread do
    sleep entry[:delay]
    use_synth entry[:synth]
    16.times { play_events subject, entry[:transpose], entry[:amp] }
  end
end
```

The piano begins alone, the pluck follows one bar later, and the lower hollow
voice arrives after another bar. Their synths and registers help you keep the
entries distinct. Once all three are sounding, the same rising-and-returning
contour occupies three successive positions in the cycle.

## Change one thing

1. Change the second delay from 4 to 2. Its first C now enters halfway through
   the leader's subject instead of against the next repetition. Identify the
   note pairs that become newly exposed, then restore the delay before testing
   another variable.
2. Set the second transposition to 7. The follower enters a fifth higher. Some
   intervals widen in pitch-class terms, yet the follower now competes with the
   leader in a closer register. Listen separately for harmonic fit and for your
   ability to follow each contour.
3. Change the subject's fourth note from 65 to 66. Because every voice reads the
   same array, the chromatic pitch appears in several overlaps and at several
   times. Mark each unstable meeting before deciding whether the source note or
   the entry plan needs revision.

## Why it works

With a four-beat delay, the follower's first position sounds against the first
position of the leader's next repetition. At two beats, that same entry sounds
against the middle of the subject. Delay therefore selects a whole map of
vertical intervals, not one isolated relationship. From the absolute starts,
you can calculate the active pair at each attack before hearing it.

Consonance is only one test of that map. A long sequence of stable thirds can
sound motionless, while individually agreeable intervals may lead both voices
to cadence at unhelpful times. A workable subject balances recognisable
contour, rhythmic life in each voice, and overlap points that imply changing
harmony across the cycle.

Transposition alters every interval in the selected map. Entry at a fifth may
preserve several scale relationships while making another tonic plausible. An
octave leaves pitch classes unchanged but clarifies register. Test delay first
and transposition second; when a collision appears, this order tells you which
parameter introduced it.

The subject array acts as immutable score data. The entry records carry delay,
transposition, synth, and amplitude because those properties describe how a
particular voice presents the subject. This is the same division used earlier
between musical form and rendering: one object remains identifiable while
several calls place it in different contexts.

Absolute `:start` values also keep the subject compatible with `play_events`
from the transcription and capstone chapters. Each repetition resets the local
cursor at the subject boundary. Entry delay remains outside the subject because
it belongs to the imitating voice, not to the melody being imitated.

## Take it further

Write an eight-beat subject and use it unchanged in a three-voice canon lasting
at least sixteen bars. Compare delays of two, four, and eight beats while all
voices remain at unison. After choosing a delay, compare unison, octave, and
fifth transpositions. Keep each entry specification independently inspectable.
In comments, identify the three overlaps where the vertical relationship is
most exposed and name the implied chord or interval at each moment. The final
choice should arise from those comparisons, not from editing a separate copy of
the subject for every voice.
